reference.source: Scriver's OMMBID / Nelson Textbook of Paediatrics
clinicalPearls: An inborn error of lysine degradation caused by deficiency of alpha-aminoadipic semialdehyde synthase (AASS), the bifunctional enzyme of the saccharopine pathway
Widely regarded as a benign biochemical variant, frequently detected incidentally, with most affected individuals being healthy
When symptoms are reported (developmental delay, hypotonia, seizures), a causal link is uncertain and co-incidental conditions must be excluded
The biochemical hallmark is elevated plasma and urinary lysine, with saccharopine accumulation when the saccharopine dehydrogenase activity of the enzyme is predominantly affected (saccharopinuria)
It should not be confused with disorders that cause true neurotoxic metabolite accumulation such as glutaric aciduria type 1
No specific treatment or lysine restriction is generally required given the benign nature, though management is individualised through a metabolic service
Diagnosis rests on plasma amino acids and urine analysis with AASS molecular confirmation
reference.pathophysiology: Lysine is chiefly degraded through the saccharopine pathway, in which the bifunctional enzyme alpha-aminoadipic semialdehyde synthase first condenses lysine with alpha-ketoglutarate to form saccharopine (lysine-ketoglutarate reductase activity) and then breaks saccharopine down (saccharopine dehydrogenase activity). Deficiency causes accumulation of lysine and, depending on which activity is more affected, saccharopine. Because these metabolites are not markedly neurotoxic, the disorder is generally biochemically benign, distinguishing it from downstream lysine-pathway defects that produce harmful organic acids.
additionalDifferentials: Glutaric aciduria type 1 and other downstream lysine degradation disorders
Other causes of a raised plasma lysine, including generalised aminoacidurias
Hyperammonaemia syndromes when lysine is elevated with other amino acids
Non-metabolic causes of incidental developmental delay
Pyridoxine-dependent epilepsy (antiquitin deficiency), which also involves the lysine pathway
Secondary amino acid abnormalities from sampling or nutritional factors
additionalInvestigations: Plasma amino acids demonstrating raised lysine
Urine amino acids and organic acids, including saccharopine assessment
Ammonia measurement to exclude a urea cycle contribution
Assessment to exclude glutaric aciduria type 1 in symptomatic children
redFlags: An encephalopathic crisis, which should prompt search for a different, harmful disorder rather than being attributed to hyperlysinaemia
Developmental regression suggesting an alternative diagnosis
Seizures out of keeping with a benign variant
reference.prognosis: Hyperlysinaemia is generally considered a benign metabolic variant with a normal prognosis in most individuals; where clinical problems coexist, an alternative or additional diagnosis should be actively sought.
pitfalls: Attributing developmental or neurological symptoms to hyperlysinaemia and missing a treatable or harmful disorder such as glutaric aciduria type 1
Imposing unnecessary lysine restriction for a benign variant
Confusing raised lysine with true urea cycle or organic acid pathology
references: Scriver's OMMBID, disorders of lysine metabolism
management: Manage as a benign inborn error that generally requires no specific treatment or dietary lysine restriction
Confirm the biochemical pattern of raised plasma and urinary lysine and undertake AASS molecular testing
Exclude disorders causing genuinely neurotoxic metabolites, in particular glutaric aciduria type 1, in any symptomatic child
Measure ammonia to exclude a urea-cycle contribution when interpreting the amino acid profile
Reassure and avoid overinvestigation once serious alternatives are excluded, seeking an additional diagnosis if clinical problems persist
Offer genetic counselling given autosomal recessive inheritance
Individualise ongoing care and developmental assessment through a metabolic service
